claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight HEA is a non-equilibrium, metastable solid solution.
Mg and the other constituent elements are initially uniformly distributed.
Thermal exposure drives Mg-rich intermetallic precipitation from the metastable solid solution.
Mg-rich intermetallics form through diffusion-controlled nucleation and growth.
Mg diffuses and segregates out of the solid solution during thermal exposure.
Mg-rich precipitates preferentially form at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
Intermetallic phase separation changes the local distribution of elements needed to form protective oxide layers.
Element redistribution and depletion can influence oxidation kinetics and produce non-protective oxides.
Discontinuous intermetallic networks and local depletion of protective elements degrade corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
A continuous precipitate-derived barrier phase could instead enhance corrosion or oxidation resistance.
Service-like aging will produce coexistence of retained solid-solution regions and Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
The aged microstructural inhomogeneity will correlate with reduced corrosion resistance.
Aged samples will develop non-protective, discontinuous oxide scales at precipitate boundaries.
Rapid quenching will preserve the original metastable solid-solution state.
Rapidly quenched samples will retain baseline oxidation and corrosion resistance.
Transformation effects become significant above approximately 550 degrees Celsius when exposure lasts tens of minutes to hours.
Lower temperatures or rapid quenching should largely preserve the initial state.
A controlled slow ramp with holds up to approximately 900 degrees Celsius can be compared with rapid quenching.
HTXRD, TEM/SEM, oxide cross-section analysis, TGA, and corrosion testing can measure phase evolution and associated performance changes.
